dek: Games are averaging 2.92 million viewers through two weeks, the best start on record.

slides.label: The Numbers
slides.text: Through Week 2, NBA games averaged *2.92 million* viewers, up 25% from last year.

slides.label: Platform Breakdown
slides.text: *Prime Video* nearly doubled: 2.38 million viewers, up from 961,000 last year.

slides.label: NBC's Numbers
slides.text: NBC with Peacock drew 4.76 million; strip one new timeslot and it's still up 15%.

slides.label: Biggest Games
slides.text: Top draws so far: *Lakers-Warriors* (2.67M) and *Knicks-76ers* (2.58M) on Prime.

slides.label: Old Narrative
slides.text: Two seasons ago, ratings really were down, averaging *1.76 million* at midseason.

slides.label: What Changed
slides.text: The league signed an *11-year media deal*, spreading games across NBC, Peacock, ESPN and Prime.

slides.label: The Asterisks
slides.text: Nielsen's new counting method and shifting streaming trackers mean *the ruler changed too*.

slides.label: The Den's Take
slides.text: The audience didn't leave, *it moved*. The real question is what people watch for next.

caption_instagram:
NBA viewership is up 25% this season, not down, despite the narrative you keep hearing. Through the first two weeks of 2026-27, games across NBC, ESPN and Prime Video averaged 2.92 million viewers, the best start on record.

The ratings-are-down talk is real, it's just old. Two seasons ago, before the league's new 11-year media deal, national games were actually averaging 1.76 million, down 5%. Then the NBA spread across more platforms people already open, and the audience followed. Prime Video nearly doubled its numbers, NBC's games pulled in millions more. The games that pop still have names attached: Lakers, Warriors, Knicks.

The audience didn't leave. It moved. The real question is what keeps it watching next.

The NBA 'ratings are down' story everyone keeps repeating is actually last year's story, maybe the year before that. This fall, games on NBC, ESPN and Prime Video are averaging 2.92 million viewers through two weeks, up 25% and the best start on record, according to Sports Media Watch.

The lesson isn't really about basketball. It's about distribution. Two seasons ago, before the league's new 11-year media deal, national ratings actually were sliding. Then the NBA put more games on platforms people already pay for, Prime Video, NBC, Peacock, and the audience showed up where it already was.

For founders and operators, the takeaway is the same one the Den keeps coming back to: an audience that looks gone has often just moved. The real work isn't proving people still care. It's building something worth watching when they do.
